question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is monochromatic so the 9 top-facing stickers give no information about the permutation. You have to read the U-layer pieces from their side colours.

There are 4 U-layer edges and 4 U-layer corners to distinguish, and each piece is uniquely identified by at least one of its non-U stickers that is visible on the four side faces. In practice that is one visible side sticker per edge and one visible side sticker per corner, 4 + 4 = 8 non-top-facing stickers in total. With those 8 side stickers you can read the full 4-cycle / 2-cycle pattern of edges and corners and therefore name the PLL case unambiguously.

2.text:
After an OLL the U face is monochromatic.  All the information that
distinguishes one permutation of the last layer from another is therefore
carried by the side stickers that belong to the U–layer.

The U–layer is made of

* 4 U–edges UF,UR,UB,UL : 1 side sticker each which is visible on F,R,B,L,
* 4 U–corners UFR,URB,UBL,ULF : 2 side stickers each, one on the first
  and one on the second side face of the corner.

i.e. 4+4×2 = 12 non–U stickers belong to the U ring.  The 9 U stickers
are all the same colour after OLL and carry no information at all.  In
the ordinary recognition that is the whole of the U-ring you have to look
at, 12 stickers on the four side faces.

Up to the whole-cube rotation that is the 8-piece information
4 edges + 4 corners.  One distinguishing side sticker per U-piece is
enough to name the piece, so the permutation can in fact be named by
1 sticker per piece, i.e. 8 distinguishing non-U stickers, and with the
corner–edge parity relation three corners + three edges, six stickers,
already forces the fourth piece.  This is the 12-sticker U-ring that is
normally quoted as the 8-piece, 4+4 sticker recognition of a PLL.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is a solid colour so the permutation information is entirely carried by the side stickers of the U-layer pieces. There are 8 pieces on the U layer, 4 corners and 4 edges, and each piece must be identified by at least one non-U sticker in order to be able to read the corner permutation and the edge permutation separately. In practice you can read a corner by its two side stickers and an edge by its single side sticker, so the minimal identifying set is one distinguishing sticker per piece, i.e. 4 corner side stickers + 4 edge side stickers = 8 non-top-facing stickers. Once those 8 side colours are known the whole PLL class is fixed, and any fewer would leave at least two pieces ambiguous between the 21 PLL cases.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8 non-top-facing stickers.

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the PLL is not read off the top at all. Identification has to come from the side colours of the U-layer pieces. In practice recognition is done from two adjacent side faces, and you need the side information for all four U-layer corners and the four U-layer edges.

Each U-layer corner contributes two distinct side stickers and each U-layer edge contributes one side sticker that is visible on the side you are looking at. To be able to tell the 21 PLL permutations apart you need the colour pair for each of the four corners together with the four edge colours, i.e. the eight distinct non-top stickers that belong to the U layer. Looking at the front and right top rows you can see those eight stickers, and with fewer than that two different PLL cases remain indistinguishable. In a standard two-face view that is the information you are actually using to name the case.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is monochromatic, so the U stickers themselves carry no information about which cubie is where. A PLL case is a permutation of the 8 U-layer cubies, 4 edges and 4 corners. In practice you identify a case by the colour pattern that the U-layer shows on the side faces.

Each of the 4 U-layer edges is identified by the single side sticker that is visible on the front/right/back/left face. Each of the 4 U-layer corners is identified by at least one of its two side stickers. One side sticker per cubie is enough to tell the cubie apart from the other seven, so in the worst case you need to be able to read one side sticker for all 8 cubies.

That is 4 edge stickers + 4 corner stickers = 8 non-U stickers. Once those eight side colours are known the edge permutation and the corner permutation are both fixed, and the 21 PLL classes are uniquely distinguished.

3.text:
In CFOP the U face is already solved after OLL, so the whole information
which PLL you are looking at is in the permutation of the eight U–layer
pieces.  The U–layer peripheral is

* 4 U–edges – 1 non–U sticker per edge,
* 4 U–corners – 2 non–U stickers per corner,

i.e. 4 + 2×4 = 12 non–U stickers on the U–layer periphery.
In information theoretic terms one of the 12 is a parity dependent
redundancy, so 7 independent non–U stickers are enough to fix the
permutation of the eight U pieces.  In the normal language of the
method this is phrased as one readable side sticker per U–piece, i.e.
4 edge side stickers and 4 corner side stickers, 8 non–U stickers in
all.  Up to the one parity redundancy this is the 7 independent
non–U stickers that are in fact read for a PLL recognition, the
12–sticker U–periphery being the full physical set.  This is the
usual 4+4 = 8 sticker, 7 independent sticker, read for a PLL.

11.text:
In CFOP the U face is already solved after the OLL step. The U face is
therefore monochromatic and carries no distinguishing information for the
last layer permutation. What distinguishes one PLL from another is the
identity of the four U edges and the four U corners which are now sitting
in the U slice.

The U slice is made up of

* 4 U edges : 1 U sticker + 1 side sticker per piece,
* 4 U corners : 1 U sticker + 2 side stickers per piece.

Hence the U slice contains 4+4 = 8 pieces, 8 U stickers and

* 4 edge side stickers
* 8 corner side stickers

$4+8=12$

non-U stickers. Those 12 side stickers are the information bearing
stickers of a PLL. Once you know the colour of the 12 side stickers of the
U slice you know the corner permutation and the edge permutation of the
last layer and you know which of the 21 PLL classes you are in.

In practice you never have to read the whole 12 sticker set.  The edge
permutation is determined up to rotation by three distinct U edge side
stickers and the corner permutation is determined up to rotation by three
distinct U corner side stickers.  Six non-U stickers, three edges and
three corners, are therefore a theoretical sufficient set, and in normal
recognition four to eight of the twelve U-slice side stickers are more
than enough to name the case.  The textbook “you have to read the U slice’’
is the 12 side stickers of the U layer, 4 edge + 8 corner, i.e. the whole
non-U part of the U slice.  This is what is normally quoted as the 12
non-top stickers that encode a PLL.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is solid, so the permutation information is not on the top at all. You have to read the last layer from the lateral stickers. There are eight distinct U-layer pieces to distinguish, four corners and four edges. A corner can only be told apart from the other three by its two side colours and an edge can only be told apart by its single side colour. In practice that means you need a distinguishing side sticker for each piece, i.e. one lateral sticker per corner and one lateral sticker per edge. That is 4 + 4 = 8 non-U stickers in the minimal distinguishable set, and with those eight you can read off the corner permutation and the edge permutation and therefore name the PLL case.

4.text:
In CFOP the U–layer is already oriented, U is monochrome and the only thing
that is left to know is the permutation of the 8 U–pieces.  The U–layer
itself carries no information on the U–face so that all of the information
has to be taken from the side of the U–ring.

The U–ring is

* 4 U–edges : 1 side sticker per piece, 4 stickers
* 4 U–corners : 2 side stickers per piece, 8 stickers

i.e. 12 physical non–U stickers belong to the last layer, 4+8.  In
information terms you only have to read one identifier per piece.  The
edge of a U–edge is identified by its single side colour and a U–corner
is identified – up to the solved orientation – by the colour that you see
on the side of the cube.  Hence, up to the usual U–rotation equivalence,
the permutation is completely fixed by the 4 edge side colours and the 4
corner side colours, i.e. by 8 distinct side identifiers.  That is the
12 stickers of the U–ring, 4×1 for the edges and 4×2 for the corners,
normally quoted as the 8 pieces 4E+4C that have to be read.  In the
literal physical count this is the 12 non–U stickers of the U–ring,
essentially the 8–piece, 4+4 sticker read that is used in ordinary PLL
recognition.

6.text:
In CFOP the $U$-face is already solved so the whole $U$–information which you
can get from the top of the cube is trivial.  The whole information that is
carried by a PLL is the information which is carried by the 12 side
stickers of the $U$-layer

* $4$ $U$-edges, one side sticker per edge;
* $4$ $U$-corners, two side stickers per corner,

i.e. $4\times 1+4\times 2=12$ non-$U$ stickers.  Once the 12 stickers of the
$U$-layer are known the permutation of the four $U$-edges and the
permutation of the four $U$-corners is known and hence the 21 PLL
classes, up to an AUF, are known.

Because the permutation of $n$ objects is fixed by the position of $n-1$
of them the information is redundant.  In particular an edge
permutation is fixed by the three edges which are seen and a corner
permutation is fixed by three corners, the fourth being forced by
parity.  Information theoretically this is

* $3$ $U$-edge side stickers, the fourth edge being forced, and
* $3$ $U$-corner side stickers, i.e. six distinct corner-side stickers,
the fourth corner being forced,

so that in the absolute worst case seven distinct non-$U$ stickers of
the $U$-layer are enough to make the 21 PLL classes pairwise
distinguishable.  This is the number which is normally quoted in the
literature as ``seven side stickers of the last layer''.  If the two
side stickers of a corner are counted separately this is the familiar
statement that you have to look at the four edge stickers and at least
one side sticker of each of the four $U$-corners, i.e. eight distinct
$U$-layer side stickers, the 12 side stickers of the $U$-layer being
the complete information.  The eight-sticker form is the one which is
usually taught as $4$ edges $+$ $4$ corners, the seventh/eighth sticker
being the one which is implied by parity.  This is the $12$-sticker
$U$-layer information that is normally reduced in practice to the
seven/eight stickers which you actually have to read. ∎

10.text:
In CFOP the U face is already solved when you get to the permutation step.
In particular the nine U stickers are all the same colour and carry no
information about the permutation. All of the information about the
permutation of the last layer is carried by the side stickers of the
U layer.

The U layer is made up of 

* 4 U edges, each of which has one sticker on U and one sticker on a
side face, and
* 4 U corners, each of which has one sticker on U and two stickers on
side faces,

so that on the top layer there are

4 × 1 = 4 side stickers belonging to the U edges
4 × 2 = 8 side stickers belonging to the U corners

i.e. 12 distinct non-U stickers, the whole top row of the four side
faces.  That is the information content of a PLL.  In practice the
information is normally spoken of piece-wise: 4 edge side stickers
and one distinguishing side sticker per corner, i.e. 4+4 = 8
independent non-U colour positions, the other four corner side stickers
being forced by the piece identity once the U layer is oriented.  The
12 side stickers of the U layer are the 12 non-U stickers you have to
inspect if you want the whole top-layer colour information in hand,
which is the usual 8-piece 4 edge + 4 corner description of a PLL.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 4

In CFOP the U layer is already oriented after OLL, so PLL is a pure permutation problem. The top face pattern gives you the permutation class up to rotation, but the chirality of the permutation remains ambiguous until you have an absolute reference for the cube. That reference is supplied by the side colours of the U layer pieces. In practice you only need the side colour information of the four U-layer corners – one visible side sticker per corner on the front/right view – to break the rotational symmetry and resolve the mirror pairs such as J/Jb, N/Nb, etc. Once the four corner side colours are known the edge permutation is already implied by the top face, so no further non-top stickers are required to name the PLL case uniquely.

12.text:
On the solved OLL the whole U face is monochromatic. The only thing that
still carries information is the U slice.  Up to a U-turn the U-slice is

* 4 U-edges, one side facelet each  – 4 facelets
* 4 U-corners, two side facelets each – 8 facelets

i.e.  4+8 = 12 non-U facelets on the U-slice, 8 distinct U-pieces.  
In recognition language that is the U-ring.  The four edges are already
identified by their single side sticker, the four corners are identified
by one side sticker each, so eight distinct side stickers are enough
to name the 4 edge pieces and the 4 corner pieces and hence to name the
permutation up to a U-rotation.  Counting facelets the complete ring is
the 12 side facelets of the U-slice, the eight piece-identities that are
normally quoted as the four edge side stickers + four corner side
stickers.  This is the information that is actually used in PLL
recognition; the remaining 4 corner side facelets are the mates of the
four that are read.  The 12 facelets are the 12 non-U stickers of the
U-layer.

8.text:
In CFOP the top layer is oriented before you ever get to PLL.

After an OLL the U face is solid.  In particular the eight stickers

```
U1 U2 U3 U4   and   U5 U6 U7 U8
```

which belong to the four U edges and the four U corners are all the
colour of the U centre. Up to a whole cube rotation the U face is
therefore information free for a permutation.  The whole of the
permutation information of the last layer is carried by the side
colours of the U layer.

The U layer is

* 4 U edges, 1 side sticker per edge, 4 stickers;
* 4 U corners, 2 side stickers per corner, 8 stickers.

i.e. 12 stickers of the cube which are not U stickers, 8 distinct
U-layer pieces.  In ordinary recognition you read the four edge side
colours and the four corner side colours, i.e. the eight pieces of the
U layer, the 12 side stickers of the U layer in the full view.  Up to
AUF the top face itself gives no information at all for a PLL, so in
the usual language you recognise a PLL with zero U-face information and
with the side colours of the U layer.  With the usual book-keeping
this is quoted as the eight non-U pieces of the U layer,  four edge
side stickers + four corner side stickers, 12 stickers in the complete
U layer, 7–8 of which are already enough in information theoretic
terms to separate the 21 PLL classes.  In particular the U face itself
is monochromatic after OLL and is not used for PLL recognition at all.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochromatic, so the nine U stickers carry no permutation information at all. The whole PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces, four edges and four corners.

Each U-layer edge is identified by the single side sticker that sticks out on F/R/B/L. Each U-layer corner is identified by its two side stickers, one on each adjacent side face. In recognition you need a distinguishing side colour for every piece, otherwise you cannot separate the corner permutation from the edge permutation and you cannot break the mirror pairs J/Jb, N/Nb, etc.

That is one visible side sticker per piece: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 non-U stickers. Those eight identifiers are enough to name the edge 4-cycle/2-cycle and the corner 3-cycle/2-cycle and therefore to name the PLL class up to AUF. The full physical U-ring is 12 non-U facelets, 4 edge + 8 corner, the extra four corner facelets being the mates of the four that are read.

The theoretical six-sticker “three edges + three corners” argument ignores the fact that in a real solve you need an unambiguous visual identifier for each piece under an arbitrary AUF and for mirror discrimination. Parity tells you the fourth piece exists, it does not tell you which side colour you are looking at. In practice you read eight distinct side identifiers, the four edge side colours and one distinguishing side colour per corner, and that is what is normally quoted as the 8-piece, 4+4 sticker recognition of a PLL.

3.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome. The nine U stickers carry no permutation
information for PLL. The whole permutation information of the last layer is
carried by the side facelets that belong to the U slice.

The U slice is

* 4 U-edges : 1 U sticker + 1 side sticker per piece
* 4 U-corners : 1 U sticker + 2 side stickers per piece

Hence on the four side faces the U-ring is

4 × 1 = 4 edge side stickers
4 × 2 = 8 corner side stickers

4 + 8 = 12 distinct non-U facelets, the whole top row of the four side
faces. Once the colours of those 12 side stickers are known the corner
permutation and the edge permutation of the last layer are known and the
21 PLL classes up to AUF are known.

In recognition language the information is spoken of piece-wise. One
distinguishing side colour is enough to name a U-piece, i.e. one side
sticker per edge and one side sticker per corner. That is the usual
4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct U-piece
identifiers that are read in practice, the 12 facelets being the complete
physical U-ring. Up to U rotation/parity 3 edges + 3 corners, 6 facelets,
7 independent facelets in total, are information theoretically sufficient
to separate the 21 cases.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome so the nine U stickers carry no permutation information. The PLL is a permutation of the eight U-slice pieces, four U edges and four U corners, and the only information you can use is on the side faces of that slice.

A U edge is identified by its single side sticker, four stickers in total. A U corner is identified by its two side stickers, but one distinguishing side sticker per corner is enough to tell the four corners apart from each other in the U slice. One sticker per piece is the piece identifier you actually read.

That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U stickers that have to be readable to name the corner permutation and the edge permutation unambiguously. In the full U-ring there are 12 side facelets, 4 for the edges and 8 for the corners, and the extra four corner stickers are the mates of the four you already read.

Counting three edges and three corners as a theoretical minimal set is only a relative permutation. With the fourth piece left out by parity you still have an AUF ambiguity and you cannot resolve mirror pairs such as J/Jb, N/Nb, T etc. without an absolute reference for the whole U slice. In practice recognition is done with one identifying side sticker per U piece, i.e. the eight non-top stickers of the U layer, and that is the set that fixes the PLL class up to whole-cube rotation.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome, so the U stickers carry zero PLL information. The whole case is the permutation of the 8 U-layer pieces.

That is 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners. An edge is identified by its single side sticker, a corner by at least one of its two side stickers. In a real solve you do not get to choose an ideal theoretical set of three edges and three corners; you are reading the last layer from the side faces and you need to be able to name each of the eight pieces unambiguously up to AUF.

If you only have three edge side stickers you still have to distinguish the fourth edge from the three remaining possibilities, and the same for corners. More importantly the mirror pairs J/Jb, N/Nb, R/Rb etc are not resolved by three corners alone: you need the side colour information for all four corners to break the chirality / mirror ambiguity, and you need all four edge side colours to read the edge permutation and its relative orientation to the corners.

In practice recognition is quoted as one distinguishing sticker per piece: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 non-U stickers. The other four corner side stickers are the mates of the four you read and are forced once the piece identity is known, which is why the full physical U-ring is 12 non-U stickers. Eight is the operational minimum that guarantees you can name the corner permutation and the edge permutation and therefore the 21 PLL classes without having to assume you happened to see the “right” three edges and three corners.

Fewer than eight leaves at least one piece undetermined and the case remains ambiguous under U rotation and mirror equivalence.

10.text:
After OLL the U face is monochromatic. The nine U stickers therefore carry
zero permutation information for PLL and the whole PLL class is carried by
the side stickers of the U-slice, the U-ring.

Physically the U-ring is

* 4 U-edges : 1 side sticker per edge = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners : 2 side stickers per corner = 8 non-U stickers

4+8 = 12 non-U stickers in total on the four side faces. That is the complete
physical information bearing set of the last layer.

For recognition the U-ring is read piece wise. An edge is uniquely identified
by its single side sticker and a corner is uniquely identified up to U
orientation by one of its two side stickers. One distinguishing side sticker
per U-piece is enough to name the piece, i.e.

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U identifiers

for the 8 U-layer pieces. With those eight side colours the edge
permutation and the corner permutation are both fixed up to an AUF and the
21 PLL classes are pairwise distinguishable. The remaining four corner side
stickers are the mates of the four that are read and are forced once the
piece identity is known.

In information-theoretic terms the permutation of four edges is fixed by
three edges and the permutation of four corners is fixed by three corners,
so six distinct side identifiers, seven independent non-U stickers with
parity, are the absolute lower bound. The textbook teaching form is the
8-piece, 4+4, description, viz. the 12 side stickers of the U-ring read as
eight distinguishing non-U stickers.

6.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome. The U facelets therefore carry no
permutation information for PLL and the whole PLL class is contained in
the U-slice.

The U-slice is

* 4 U-edges : 1 U sticker + 1 side sticker per piece
* 4 U-corners : 1 U sticker + 2 side stickers per piece

so that physically the U-ring has

4×1 = 4 edge side facelets
4×2 = 8 corner side facelets

4+8 = 12 non-U facelets, the whole top row of the four side faces,
the 12 stickers that belong to the U layer.

For recognition that 12 facelet set is redundant.  An edge is identified
by its single side colour and a U-corner is already oriented by OLL, so
up to the solved orientation a corner is identified by one of its two
side colours.  Hence one distinguishing side identifier per U-piece is
enough:

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U
stickers

and with those eight side colours the 4-cycle / 2-cycle pattern of the
four U-edges and the four U-corners is fixed up to AUF and the 21 PLL
classes are distinguished.  With the corner–edge parity relation the
fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced, so information-theoretically

operational statement being the familiar 4+4 = 8 piece, 12 facelet U-ring

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is solid and carries no permutation information. The PLL is the permutation of the 8 U-layer cubies, 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.

So you need one distinguishing non-U sticker for each of the 8 U-pieces, 4 edge + 4 corner = 8 non-top-facing stickers. With those eight you can read the edge permutation and the corner permutation separately and name the 21 PLL classes up to AUF.

The U slice is 8 pieces: 4 U edges and 4 U corners. An edge is identified by its single side sticker, a corner is identified by at least one of its two side stickers. In recognition you need a distinguishing side colour for every piece you want to name.

That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 non-U stickers. Once those eight side colours are known the edge permutation and the corner permutation are both fixed up to AUF and the 21 PLL classes are uniquely distinguished.

The 12 physical side facelets of the U ring, 4 edge + 8 corner, are the whole ring, and the four extra corner facelets are just the mates of the four corner identifiers you already read. The information-theoretic 6 sticker comment is a theoretical counting argument about parity forcing the fourth piece once the other three pieces are known. In practice you cannot rely on that inference for reliable real-time recognition and for breaking the J/Jb, N/Nb mirror ambiguities. You need a visible side identifier for each of the eight U-layer pieces, i.e. the usual 8-piece 4+4 description of a PLL. That is why the standard teaching is 8 non-top stickers, the 12-facet U-ring reduced to eight independent identifiers.
public_text.9:
After OLL the U face is solid and carries no permutation information. The PLL is the permutation of the 8 U-layer cubies, 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.

Identification has to come from the side stickers of the U-slice. A U-edge is identified by its single side sticker, 4 stickers in total. A U-corner is identified by its side colours; at least one visible side sticker per corner is needed to tell that corner apart from the other three U-corners. That is 4 distinguishing corner side stickers.

So you need one distinguishing non-U sticker for each of the 8 U-pieces, 4 edge + 4 corner = 8 non-top-facing stickers. With those eight you can read the edge permutation and the corner permutation separately and name the 21 PLL classes up to AUF.

The 12 physical non-U stickers of the U-ring are 4 edge + 8 corner facelets. The 3+3 = 6 information-theoretic lower bound is a counting argument about parity: the fourth edge is forced by the other three and the fourth corner is forced by the other three. That is a theoretical redundancy. In practice it is not operational. Recognition has to resolve mirror pairs J/Jb, N/Nb, T/Tb etc. and it has to be stable under the U-turn/AUF equivalence you can apply before naming the case. You cannot rely on inferring the fourth piece from parity alone without a fixed absolute reference for the cube, and you cannot rely on leaving a corner or an edge unread because the two pieces you would be inferring are the ones that distinguish the mirror. 

Hence the set you actually read in recognition is the 8 piece identifiers, 4 edge side stickers and 4 corner side stickers, the complete 12-sticker U-ring being the physical superset. Fewer than eight distinct non-U positions leaves at least two U-pieces unnamed and leaves two PLL cases indistinguishable in a real table.
public_text.13:
After OLL the U face is monochrome, so the PLL is not read off the top at all. The whole permutation information is in the side colours of the 8 U-layer cubies.

That is 4 U edges and 4 U corners. An edge is identified by its single side sticker, a corner is identified by its side stickers. In ordinary recognition you need a distinguishing side colour for each of the 8 pieces, otherwise the corner or edge permutation is not fixed.

In practice that is taught as 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 non-top-facing stickers. Those are the eight piece-identifiers you have to be able to read. The U-ring physically contains 12 non-U facelets, 4 for the edges and 8 for the corners, and the four extra corner facelets are the mates of the four you read.

The information-theoretic comment that three edges + three corners, six stickers, is enough to force the fourth by parity is true in the abstract, but it is not what you have to guarantee you can see in a real solve. With three corners and three edges you still have AUF / mirror ambiguity and you are relying on inferring the missing piece rather than actually identifying it. For an unambiguous, worst-case naming of the 21 PLL classes you need a distinguishing side sticker for every U piece, i.e. the usual 4 + 4 = 8 independent non-U identifiers, the 12-sticker U-ring in its full physical form.

The permutation information of a PLL is the permutation of the 8 U-slice
cubies

* 4 U-edges : 1 U sticker + 1 side sticker per piece
* 4 U-corners : 1 U sticker + 2 side stickers per piece

so that the U-ring physically contains

4 × 1 = 4 edge side stickers
4 × 2 = 8 corner side stickers

4 + 8 = 12 non-U facelets on the U-layer, the whole top row of the
four side faces.  That is the complete physical information content of a
PLL.

Piece-wise that information is redundant.  The U colour is known after
OLL so a U-edge is completely identified by its single side colour and a
U-corner is completely identified up to the solved orientation by one of
its two side colours.  Hence one distinguishing side sticker per U-piece
is enough to name the piece.  In normal recognition language this is

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U
identifiers,

the 4+4 = 8 piece description of a PLL.  The other four corner side
facelets are the mates of the four that are read and are forced by piece
identity; information theoretically 7 independent non-U stickers, 3
edges + 3 corners up to rotation, already fix the permutation of the 8
U-pieces and therefore the 21 PLL classes up to AUF.  The 12 facelets of
the U-ring are the 12 non-U stickers that are normally quoted as the
8-piece 4E+4C read for PLL.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion has converged on the structure of PLL information after OLL in CFOP.

The U face is monochromatic, 9 U stickers carry zero permutation information. All PLL information is in the U-slice side facelets.

Physically the U-ring is:
* 4 U-edges, 1 side sticker each = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners, 2 side stickers each = 8 non-U stickers
Total physical non-U facelets on the U-ring = 12. This is the complete information-bearing set normally quoted as the U-ring.

Operationally the information is piece-wise redundant. An edge is uniquely identified by its single side sticker. A U-corner is oriented after OLL, so up to U orientation one of its two side stickers is enough to name the piece. Hence one distinguishing side sticker per U-piece is enough:
4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers for the 8 U-layer pieces.
With those 8 side colours the edge permutation and corner permutation are fixed up to AUF and the 21 PLL classes are pairwise distinguishable. The remaining 4 corner side stickers are the mates of the 4 read and are forced by piece identity.

Information-theoretic lower bound is often cited: permutation of 4 edges fixed by 3 edges, permutation of 4 corners fixed by 3 corners, so 6 distinct side identifiers, 7 independent non-U stickers with parity, are sufficient in the abstract. The current round pushes back on using this as an operational minimum: three corners + three edges alone leaves AUF / mirror ambiguity and does not reliably resolve mirror pairs J/Jb, N/Nb, R/Rb etc. Real recognition needs a distinguishing side colour for every U piece to break chirality and to be stable under arbitrary AUF.

Colleague 14 has moved from the earlier 4-sticker outlier to the 8-sticker operational view. Colleagues 1,7,9,13,5 now explicitly argue that fewer than eight leaves at least one piece undetermined and that all four corners must be referenced to resolve mirrors.

Current best synthesis remains: physically 12 non-U stickers belong to the U layer. Recognitionally the operational minimum that guarantees unambiguous naming without inference is 8 distinct side identifiers, 4 edge + 4 corner, normally taught as the 8-piece 4E+4C description of a PLL. The 12-sticker count is the full physical superset; 7 independent stickers is the information-theoretic lower bound. Unresolved wording is whether the question asks for the physical count 12 or the practical distinguishing count 8; the deliberation now leans to 8 as the must-be-seen operational set.

The physical U-ring on the four side faces is 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12 non-U facelets. That is the complete physical information content.

For recognition you need a distinguishing side colour for every U-piece, otherwise you cannot name the edge permutation and the corner permutation separately and you cannot break the mirror/chirality pairs.

* A U-edge is named by its single side sticker. You need all 4.
* A U-corner is named up to U orientation by one of its two side stickers. You need one identifying side sticker per corner, 4.

That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers. With those eight side colours the 4-cycle / 2-cycle pattern of the edges and the 3-cycle / 2-cycle pattern of the corners is fixed up to AUF and the 21 PLL classes are pairwise distinguishable. The remaining four corner side stickers are the mates of the four you read and are forced once piece identity is known, which is why the full ring is quoted as 12 facelets.

The information-theoretic 3 edges + 3 corners = 6 stickers, 7 independent with parity, is the abstract lower bound for the permutation of 8 pieces. It assumes you can always infer the fourth edge and fourth corner by parity and that you have a fixed absolute orientation reference. In real-time recognition you cannot rely on inference for mirror discrimination J/Jb, N/Nb, R/Rb etc. and for AUF stability. You need a visible side identifier for each of the eight U-layer pieces, i.e. the operational 4E+4C = 8 non-U stickers, with the 12-sticker U-ring as the physical superset. Fewer than eight leaves a piece unnamed and leaves PLL cases indistinguishable in the worst case.

11.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome. The nine U stickers carry no permutation
information for PLL. The whole PLL class is the permutation of the eight
U-slice cubies.

Physically the U-ring is the whole top row of F/R/B/L

* 4 U-edges : 1 side sticker per edge = 4 non-U facelets
* 4 U-corners : 2 side stickers per corner = 8 non-U facelets

4 + 8 = 12 non-U facelets belong to the U layer. That is the complete
physical information bearing set of a PLL.

The set is redundant up to AUF. An edge is named by its single side sticker
and a U-corner, oriented by OLL, is named up to solved orientation by one
of its two side stickers. One distinguishing side identifier per U-piece is
enough to name the piece.

In normal recognition language that is

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top
identifiers,

the usual 4E+4C 8-piece description of a PLL. With those eight side colours
the edge permutation and the corner permutation are fixed up to AUF and the
21 PLL classes are pairwise distinguishable. The remaining four corner side
stickers are the mates of the four that are read and are forced by piece
identity once OLL orientation is known.

Information theoretically the permutation of four objects is fixed by three
objects, so six distinct side identifiers, seven independent non-U stickers
with parity, is the absolute lower bound. The operational, AUF-stable,
mirror-unambiguous teaching form is the eight piece identifiers, i.e. the
12-facelet U-ring read as 4+4 = 8 non-top stickers.

8.text:
After OLL the U face is monochromatic and carries no permutation
information.  The whole of a PLL is the permutation of the eight U-slice
cubies.

U-slice side information

* 4 U-edges : 1 side sticker per edge on F/R/B/L  → 4 non-U facelets
* 4 U-corners : 2 side stickers per corner          → 8 non-U facelets

the U-ring.  That is the complete physical information bearing set of a

uniquely named by its single side sticker and a U-corner is already

fix the edge permutation and the corner permutation and to distinguish

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top
identifiers,

four corner side stickers are the mates of the four that are read and
are forced by piece identity once the U layer is oriented.  In facelet
count the U-ring is the 12 side stickers 4+8 of the U layer, of which
8 distinct non-U identifiers are the operational minimum, 7 independent
non-U stickers being the information-theoretic lower bound with parity.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I'm with the 4+4 = 8 reading that most of you have laid out.

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the nine U stickers carry no permutation information. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-slice cubies, four U-edges on F/R/B/L and four U-corners on the side faces. Physically that is the U-ring: 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12 non-U facelets on the top row of the four side faces.

Operationally the ring is redundant. An U-edge is named by its single side sticker and a U-corner is named up to AUF by one distinguishing side sticker. So one identifier per U-piece is enough to fix the edge permutation and the corner permutation and to name the 21 PLL classes up to AUF: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers.

The 3 edges + 3 corners, six sticker, information-theoretic lower bound is a neat counting argument and it's true that parity forces the fourth edge and the fourth corner once the other three are known. That is a best-case / average-case statement. “Must be seen to fully identify” is a worst-case guarantee. In a real two-face view you cannot rely on happening to have seen the right three corners and the right three edges, and you cannot rely on inferring the missing piece for real-time recognition.

Mirror/chirality is the practical blocker. J/Jb, N/Nb, R/Rb and the AUF equivalence are not resolved by three corners and three edges alone; you need a visible side identifier for each of the four corners to break mirror ambiguity and a visible side identifier for each of the four edges to read the edge cycle relative to the corners. With fewer than eight distinct side identifiers at least one U-piece is unnamed and two PLL cases remain indistinguishable in the worst case.

That is why the textbook description is eight independent non-U stickers for recognition, the 12 facelets of the U-ring being the full physical superset with the four extra corner stickers forced by piece identity once the eight identifiers are known.

public_text.13:
I'm with the 4+4 = 8 reading that most of you have laid out.

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the nine U stickers carry no permutation information. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-slice cubies, four U-edges on F/R/B/L and four U-corners on the side faces. Physically that is the U-ring: 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12 non-U facelets on the top row of the four side faces.

Operationally the ring is redundant. An U-edge is named by its single side sticker and a U-corner is named up to AUF by one distinguishing side sticker. So one identifier per U-piece is enough to fix the edge permutation and the corner permutation and to name the 21 PLL classes up to AUF: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers.

The 3 edges + 3 corners, six sticker, information-theoretic lower bound is a neat counting argument and it's true that parity forces the fourth edge and the fourth corner once the other three are known. That is a best-case / average-case statement. “Must be seen to fully identify” is a worst-case guarantee. In a real two-face view you cannot rely on happening to have seen the right three corners and the right three edges, and you cannot rely on inferring the missing piece for real-time recognition.

Mirror/chirality is the practical blocker. J/Jb, N/Nb, R/Rb and the AUF equivalence are not resolved by three corners and three edges alone; you need a visible side identifier for each of the four corners to break mirror ambiguity and a visible side identifier for each of the four edges to read the edge cycle relative to the corners. With fewer than eight distinct side identifiers at least one U-piece is unnamed and two PLL cases remain indistinguishable in the worst case.

That is why the textbook description is eight independent non-U stickers for recognition, the 12 facelets of the U-ring being the full physical superset with the four extra corner stickers forced by piece identity once the eight identifiers are known.

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the nine U stickers carry no permutation information. The whole PLL is the permutation of the eight U-slice cubies: 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.

The U-ring physically is 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12 non-U facelets on the top row of the four side faces. That 12 is the complete physical information bearing set.

In recognition you need a distinguishing side colour for each U piece you want to name, otherwise the edge permutation and the corner permutation are not fixed up to AUF and the mirror pairs are not broken. An edge is named by its single side sticker, a corner is named up to the solved orientation by one of its two side stickers. That is one identifier per piece.

One distinguishing sticker per piece is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers. With those eight you can read the 4-cycle/2-cycle pattern of the edges and the 3-cycle/2-cycle pattern of the corners and name the 21 PLL classes up to a U rotation. The remaining four corner side stickers are the mates of the four you read and are forced once the piece identity is known.

The 3 edges + 3 corners, 6 sticker, information-theoretic lower bound is correct as a counting argument about parity forcing the fourth piece. It is not a guaranteed visible set. In a real solve you cannot choose which three edges and which three corners happen to be visible after an AUF, and you cannot rely on inferring the missing piece to resolve J/Jb, N/Nb, R/Rb, T/Tb mirror ambiguities. Worst-case visibility and operational naming require a visible side identifier for each of the eight U-layer pieces.

That is why the standard teaching form is the 4+4 = 8 piece, 12 facelet U-ring recognition. The eight non-top stickers are the operational minimum that guarantees you can name the PLL without assuming you happened to see the “right” three edges and three corners.

* 4 U-corners: 2 side stickers per corner = 8 non-U stickers

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is solved in colour and carries no permutation information for PLL. The whole case is the permutation of the eight U-slice cubies, four U-edges and four U-corners, and all of that information lives on the four side faces in the top row.

Physically the U-ring is 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12 non-U facelets. That is the complete physical set.

Operationally the ring is redundant up to AUF. An U-edge is named by its single side sticker and a U-corner is named up to solved orientation by one of its two side stickers. One distinguishing side identifier per U-piece is enough to name the piece, and you need one identifier per piece to make the naming AUF-stable and mirror-unambiguous.

That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers, the usual 4E+4C teaching form. With those eight side colours the edge permutation and the corner permutation are fixed up to AUF and the 21 PLL classes are pairwise distinguishable, including the mirror pairs J/Jb, N/Nb, R/Rb.

The six sticker / seven independent sticker parity counting is a correct information-theoretic lower bound for the relative permutation of eight pieces: three edges fix the fourth by parity and three corners fix the fourth. That is an abstract counting statement about how many pieces are needed to encode the permutation, not a guaranteed visual set.

“Must be seen to fully identify” is a worst-case guarantee, not a best-case counting argument. In a real solve you cannot choose which three edges and which three corners happen to be visible after an arbitrary AUF, and you cannot rely on inferring the missing piece to break chirality. If one U-piece is left unnamed you lose the absolute reference needed to decide mirror equivalence and the case stays ambiguous under U rotation.

Hence the operational minimum that guarantees unambiguous PLL naming in the worst case is a visible, unambiguous side identifier for each of the eight U-layer pieces: 8 non-top stickers, the 12-facelet U-ring read as 4+4 distinct identifiers. Fewer than eight leaves at least one U-piece unnamed and leaves at least one pair of PLLs indistinguishable in practice.

Those eight fix the edge permutation and the corner permutation up to AUF and make the 21 PLL classes pairwise distinguishable, in particular the mirror pairs J/Jb, N/Nb, R/Rb and the AUF equivalents. The remaining four corner side stickers are forced by piece identity once the eight identifiers are known.

The 6-sticker / 7-independent-sticker parity counting is a correct information-theoretic lower bound for the abstract permutation of four objects. Three edges fix the fourth edge by parity and three corners fix the fourth corner. That is a best-case counting argument. It is not a guarantee of what you can actually see in a real solve.

“Must be seen to fully identify” is a worst-case guarantee under arbitrary AUF and real two-face visibility. You cannot choose which three edges and which three corners happen to be visible, and you cannot rely on inferring the missing piece to break chirality. If one edge or one corner is left unnamed you lose the absolute reference needed to decide J vs Jb, N vs Nb, R vs Rb, etc., and the case stays ambiguous under U rotation.

So the textbook operational minimum that is AUF-stable and mirror-unambiguous is one side identifier per U-piece: 4 edge side stickers +4 corner side stickers =8 non-top stickers, the 12-facelet U-ring read as 4E+4C. Fewer than eight leaves at least one U-piece unnamed in the worst case and leaves PLL cases indistinguishable in practice.

If one U-piece is left unnamed the case stays ambiguous in the worst case.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome, so the PLL permutation lives entirely in the U-ring on the top row of F R B L. Physically that is 4 U-edge side stickers + 8 U-corner side stickers = 12 non-U facelets, the full physical superset.

Operationally one identifier per U-piece is what makes the naming AUF-stable and mirror-unambiguous. An U-edge is named by its single side sticker, so you need all 4 edge side stickers. An U-corner, already oriented by OLL, is named up to solved orientation by one of its two side stickers, so you need one visible side identifier per corner. That is the usual 4E+4C teaching form: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers, one per U-piece.

The 3 edges + 3 corners = 6 distinct side identifiers, 7 independent non-U stickers with parity, is the correct information-theoretic counting lower bound for the abstract permutation of eight objects. It is a best-case statement that assumes you can always infer the fourth edge and fourth corner by parity and that you already have an absolute reference for chirality.

“Must be seen to fully identify” is a worst-case guarantee, not a best-case counting argument. In a real solve you cannot choose which three edges and which three corners happen to be in view after an arbitrary AUF, and you cannot rely on inferring the missing piece to break mirror equivalence in practice.
